Foggy windows and damp basements start somewhere. Here are five everyday moisture numbers, measured in pints of water.

KEY POINTS
• 3 pints: NDSU Extension says each person produces about three pints of water per day while breathing.
• About 1 pint: about one pint of moisture is introduced into a home during a 10-minute shower, and more is added when towels are drying (NDSU Extension).
• Up to 6 pints: a University of Minnesota Extension household moisture table lists clothes drying not vented outdoors, or indoor line drying, at 4.68 to 6.18 pints per load (more with a gas dryer). Dryers vented outdoors add essentially nothing.
• Nearly 3 pints: the same table lists dinner for a family of four at 1.22 pints, plus 1.58 pints if cooking with gas.
• Up to 100 pints: NDSU Extension notes that moisture coming through a concrete basement floor and walls from moist soil may create as much as 100 pints per day.
• What helps: vent clothes dryers outside and use ducted fans to exhaust moisture from kitchens and bathrooms (Oregon State University Extension). In the UMN table, boiling a 6-inch pan for 10 minutes released 0.48 pints covered vs 0.57 uncovered, and simmering released under 0.01 pints covered vs 0.13 uncovered.
Note: these are typical estimates; actual amounts vary by household.

videos.title: Rotten-Egg Smell Near a Basement Drain? 3 Sewer Gas Mistakes (Wisconsin DHS) #Shorts
videos.description:
Smelling rotten eggs near a basement drain? That's often sewer gas. Three mistakes to avoid, using Wisconsin health guidance.

KEY POINTS
• Sewer gas 101: Wisconsin DHS says highly toxic components of sewer gas include hydrogen sulfide and ammonia. Sewer gas can enter a home through a floor drain, from a leaking or blocked plumbing roof vent, or through foundation cracks if gases are in the soil next to the house.
• Mistake 1 – Forgetting seldom-used drains: DHS advises flushing floor and sink drains with water to prevent the traps in sewer pipes from drying out.
• Why traps matter: the Illinois Department of Public Health notes that in the home, exposure may occur because of faulty plumbing, and sewer drains with dry traps can allow hydrogen sulfide gas to enter.
• Mistake 2 – Stopping at the drain: DHS suggests following the odor to its entry point, then checking for a blocked rooftop plumbing vent. If the leak is behind a wall, you may need a plumber; some local health departments offer home inspections.
• Mistake 3 – Relying on your nose alone: IDPH says you can smell hydrogen sulfide at levels lower than those that may cause health effects, but at higher levels your nose can become overwhelmed and you cannot smell it.
• Strong odor indoors: if you believe there are high concentrations of sewer gas in an enclosed space, DHS says evacuate, call the fire department, and avoid creating an ignition source such as a spark from an electrical appliance, match, or lighter. If you have symptoms and suspect a sewer gas leak, see a doctor.

SOURCES
Wisconsin DHS – Air: Sewer Gas: https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/air/sewergas.htm
Illinois Department of Public Health – Hydrogen Sulfide Gas: https://www.idph.state.il.us/envhealth/factsheets/hydrogensulfide.htm

videos.title: Broke a CFL Bulb? EPA's Step-by-Step Cleanup (and Why You Shouldn't Vacuum) #Shorts
videos.description:
Just dropped a curly fluorescent bulb? CFLs contain a small amount of mercury, so EPA lays out a specific cleanup routine. Here it is, step by step.

KEY POINTS
• Step 1 – Clear and air the room: have people and pets leave the room, open a window or door to the outdoors, and leave the room for 5–10 minutes (EPA).
• Step 2 – Shut off the HVAC: shut off the central forced-air heating/air conditioning system, if you have one.
• Step 3 – Scoop, don't vacuum: carefully scoop up glass fragments and powder using stiff paper or cardboard, then use sticky tape such as duct tape to pick up remaining small pieces. EPA says do not vacuum during cleanup unless broken glass remains after all other cleanup steps; vacuuming could spread mercury-containing powder or vapor (available information on this is limited).
• Step 4 – Wipe and seal: wipe hard surfaces with damp paper towels or disposable wet wipes, and place debris in a glass jar with a metal lid. A plastic bag will not prevent mercury vapor from escaping, so remove any bags from the home after cleanup.
• Step 5 – Get it outside: promptly place all bulb debris and cleanup materials outdoors in a trash container or protected area, check with your local government about disposal requirements, and wash your hands.
• After: continue to air out the room and leave the HVAC system off, as practical, for several hours. For the next several times you vacuum that carpet or rug, shut off the HVAC, close doors to other rooms, open a window or door to the outside, and change the vacuum bag after each use in the area.

SOURCES
EPA – Cleaning Up a Broken CFL: https://www.epa.gov/cfl/cleaning-broken-cfl

videos.title: Pellet Stove Season in Wisconsin: A 5-Step Routine for the Stove and the Pellet Bags #Shorts
videos.description:
Firing up a pellet stove this Wisconsin winter? Here's a five-step routine for the stove and for the bags stacked beside it.

KEY POINTS
• Pellets can off-gas CO: research has shown stored bulk wood pellets can produce carbon monoxide, and a peer-reviewed study of fresh, bagged wood pellets found CO emissions too, with concentrations increasing with higher temperature and moisture in the container. Residential exposure levels in studies varied widely; most measured homes were well below life-threatening levels, but some exceeded the ASHRAE 9 ppm indoor guidance.
• Step 1 – Store with airflow: NYSERDA-funded research concluded bagged pellets should be considered a potential hazard similar to bulk pellets, requiring active ventilation of the space where they're stored inside an occupied structure.
• Step 2 – Keep them cool and dry: CO emissions from bagged pellets increased with temperature and relative humidity (peer-reviewed study).
• Step 3 – Alarms on every floor: EPA Burn Wise advises installing smoke and carbon monoxide detectors on every floor of the house and outside each bedroom.
• Step 4 – Empty ash when cool: remove ashes after they've cooled and dispose of them in a metal container away from your house and flammable materials (EPA).
• Step 5 – Yearly pro cleaning: EPA says pellet stoves need regular cleaning to run efficiently and safely, and should be professionally cleaned at least once a year and inspected annually.
• Smell smoke? EPA says shut down the appliance, open a window, check that the flue is open and venting, and call a professional installer or chimney sweep.

SOURCES

videos.title: Smell Something Musty but Can't See Mold? 6 Hidden Spots EPA Says to Check #Shorts
videos.description:
Smell something musty but can't see any mold? EPA lists hidden spots worth checking. Here's a six-spot checklist.

KEY POINTS
• Why suspect hidden mold: EPA says you may suspect hidden mold if a building smells moldy but you cannot see the source, or if you know there has been water damage.
• 1 – Behind wall coverings: mold may hide on the back side of drywall, wallpaper, or paneling. EPA notes materials such as drywall with vinyl wallpaper or wood paneling may act as vapor barriers, trapping moisture underneath.
• 2 – Above ceiling tiles: the top side of ceiling tiles and roof materials above them (due to roof leaks or insufficient insulation).
• 3 – Under carpet and pad: the underside of carpets and pads. EPA's mold course notes carpet backing or padding must be dried in addition to the carpet, or mold will likely result.
• 4 – Around pipes: areas inside walls around leaking or condensing pipes.
• 5 – Behind furniture: the surface of walls behind furniture, where condensation forms.
• 6 – HVAC spots: poorly draining condensate drain pans inside air handling units and porous thermal or acoustic liners inside ductwork.
• Don't rip it open: investigating hidden mold requires caution. EPA warns that removing wallpaper can lead to a massive release of spores if mold is growing underneath; if you believe you have a hidden mold problem, consider hiring an experienced professional.

SOURCES
EPA – A Brief Guide to Mold, Moisture and Your Home: https://www.epa.gov/mold/brief-guide-mold-moisture-and-your-home

videos.title: MERV Ratings Decoded: What 11, 13 and HEPA Really Catch #Shorts
videos.description:
That number on your furnace filter has a specific meaning. Here's how MERV works, by the numbers.

KEY POINTS
• MERV (Minimum Efficiency Reporting Value) runs from 1 to 16 and reports a filter's ability to capture particles between 0.3 and 10 microns (ASHRAE Standard 52.2).
• The smallest tested range, 0.3–1 µm, makes up a significant fraction of PM2.5 — but filters are only explicitly tested on it at MERV 11 and above.
• MERV 11: at least 20% removal of 0.3–1 µm particles.
• MERV 13: at least 50% for 0.3–1 µm, at least 85% for 1–3 µm, and at least 90% for 3–10 µm.
• HEPA is rated separately (not on the MERV scale) and can theoretically remove at least 99.97% of 0.3-µm particles; true HEPA filters usually aren't installed in residential HVAC and would likely require professional modification.
• EPA: choose at least MERV 13, or as high as your system fan and filter slot can accommodate; consult an HVAC technician if unsure, and follow the manufacturer's replacement schedule.

videos.title: Do Houseplants Clean Indoor Air? What 30 Years of Studies Show #Shorts
videos.description:
Can a few houseplants purify the air at home? A review of 30 years of chamber studies did the math.

KEY POINTS
• Classic "plants clean air" results came from small sealed chambers (often 1 m³ or less) where a single VOC was injected and tracked for hours or days.
• Cummings & Waring (J Expo Sci Environ Epidemiol, 2020) reviewed 12 published studies and translated 196 results into clean air delivery rate (CADR), the standard air-cleaner metric.
• Median single-plant CADR was about 0.023 m³/h — meaning 10–1,000 plants per square meter of floor space would be needed to match the VOC removal that normal outdoor-air exchange already provides.
• The American Lung Association translates that to roughly 680 plants in a 1,500 sq ft home.
• Caveat: real-home studies are few, and most did not measure ventilation, so isolating any small plant effect is difficult. Plants may still have well-being benefits.
• EPA: source control is usually the most effective way to improve indoor air; increasing outdoor air is another approach.

videos.title: Duct Cleaning Myths vs Facts (What the EPA Actually Says) #Shorts
videos.description:
A duct cleaning company busting duct cleaning myths — here's what the EPA's homeowner guidance really says.

KEY POINTS
• EPA: duct cleaning has never been shown to actually prevent health problems, and studies don't conclusively show dust levels drop after cleaning.
• A light amount of household dust in ducts is normal; much of it sticks to duct surfaces and doesn't necessarily enter living spaces.
• EPA says consider cleaning when there is substantial visible mold in the system, vermin (rodents or insects), or excessive dust and debris — including particles released from supply registers.
• Fix the underlying cause (leaks, moisture, pests) before cleaning, or the problem will likely recur.
• Research has not demonstrated the effectiveness of biocides and sealants in duct cleaning; no biocides are registered by EPA for internally insulated (fiberglass-lined) ducts.
• Prevention: use the highest-efficiency filter your system's manufacturer recommends, change filters regularly, and have fuel-burning furnaces, stoves and fireplaces inspected before each heating season.
• Ask any provider to show you the mold or debris they say they found.

videos.title: Winter Humidity by the Numbers: 30, 50, 60 (Wisconsin Homes) #Shorts
videos.description:
Three numbers decide whether your winter air is too dry, just right, or feeding dust mites and window sweat.

KEY POINTS
• EPA: keep indoor relative humidity below 60%, ideally 30–50%.
• Dust mites take in water from humid air. In a 17-month Ohio study (Arlian et al., 2001), homes held under 51% RH saw live mites drop about 98% and ended with allergen levels more than 10× lower than humid homes.
• Cold-climate guidance (University of Minnesota research): lower your indoor RH as it gets colder outside — roughly under 40% at 20–40°F, under 30% at 0–10°F, and about 20% or less at −10 to −20°F. Exact limits vary with your windows and home.
• UMN Extension lists winter window condensation as a sign of excess indoor moisture; if the inside of the glass is wet, turn the humidifier down.
• EPA humidifier care: empty, wipe dry and refill portable units daily, clean them every third day, and use low-mineral (e.g., distilled) water.
• Measure with an inexpensive hygrometer instead of guessing.
